newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH boosts Grand Met stake in puzzling gambit.
newsitem.headline: LVMH boosts Grand Met stake in puzzling gambit.

text.p: France's LVMH raised its stake in Britain's Grand Metropolitan to more than 6 percent Thursday as part of a two-pronged attack to foil the planned merger between Grand Met and Guinness, industry sources said.
Grand Met confirmed that LVMH had increased its stake to 6.29 percent from 3.2 percent after buying 125 million shares for 787.5 million pounds ($1.29 billion).
LVMH declined to comment, but the luxury goods company said earlier in the week when it first bought Grand Met shares that it had no intention of launching a takeover bid.

An industry source said LVMH was preparing to buy as much as 10 percent of Grand Met to put pressure on the British group to drop the merger plan, which faces possible U.S. and European antitrust objections, and consider LVMH's alternative proposal.

LVMH Chairman Bernard Arnault wants to create a group combining LVMH's Moet & Chandon and Hennessy brands with Guinness's Johnny Walker, Dewars and Gordon's Gin labels and, possibly, Grand Met's Smirnoff, J&B and Baileys brands.
Just how Arnault proposes to achieve that objective was not clear, but he has not lost many fights in his career.

LVMH, Guinness's largest shareholder with 14 percent, had already set out to wreck the Grand Met-Guinness merger plan by trying to buy Guinness out of their valuable joint distribution ventures, which own the rights to market Guinness brands in France, the United States and much of the Far East for 10 years.

LVMH requested arbitration from the International Chamber of Commerce last week to uphold its right to exercise those options, shredding the new Grand Met-Guinness group's distribution network, if the companies go ahead and merge.
Guinness says LVMH has no right to exercise the options, and both sides confidently say they have legal experts' backing.
An industry source said LVMH took the Grand Met stake because the arbitration could take months.
"(Arbitration) wouldn't block the merger anyway," the source said. "LVMH felt they might be more persuasive if they took a stake in Grand Met. That would oblige Grand Met to listen."
Most analysts were unclear as to LVMH's strategy. To block the merger outright, it would need more than 25 percent of Grand Met alone or with an ally.
